Weaker variability quenching in older mice is not explained by disengagement

A split-sample analysis of Fano-factor quenching on engaged trials in the IBL ageing dataset

Published

October 13, 2026

1 Original question

Do older mice show weaker quenching only because they are disengaged more often, or also when they are engaged?

During the analysis the user extended this to the other neural metrics of Zang et al.:

For firing rate, Fano factor (pre- and post-stimulus) and quenching: compare engaged and disengaged trials, then check whether the age effects in Zang et al. still hold using engaged trials only.

2 Introduction

Variability quenching. Trial-to-trial spike-count variability, measured by the Fano factor (FF, variance divided by mean), falls at stimulus onset across many cortical areas and species (Churchland et al. 2010). Zang et al. (2026) recorded mice of different ages in the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) visual decision task. They report three things in older mice:

  • higher firing rates overall;
  • a higher post-stimulus FF;
  • weaker stimulus-induced quenching (post − pre FF less negative), most clearly in visual and motor cortex, striatum and thalamic nucleus LP.

They found no age effect on pre-stimulus FF.

Engagement. Mice in this task switch between an engaged, stimulus-driven strategy and disengaged, biased strategies (Ashwood et al. 2022). A companion analysis of the same dataset fitted a two-state GLM-HMM per mouse. It found that older mice spend less time in the engaged state, and that their engaged state is weaker.

Disengaged trials might well show less quenching, since the stimulus matters less to the animal on those trials. If so, the age effect on quenching could simply reflect older mice being disengaged more often. This report tests that.

Data. ibl_aging_zang2025 v1.0.0 is a local repackaging of the OpenAlyx release used by Zang et al. It has 158 mice and 497 sessions:

  • bwm cohort: 139 mice, 92–461 days old (Brain Wide Map sessions, 12 labs);
  • lifespan cohort: 19 mice, 317–597 days old (mostly one lab).

The data hold only units that pass the three IBL single-unit quality metrics. Per-trial P(engaged) comes from the companion GLM-HMM, which was fitted separately on exploration and confirmation mice.

Age is confounded with cohort, lab, recording year, probe type and the regions sampled. One lab recorded both cohorts, which gives a within-lab contrast (bwm 140–270 d vs lifespan 317–597 d).

3 Refinement of the question

3.1 Split, units and trials

Mice were split 30/70 into exploration (48) and confirmation (110) sets. The split was stratified by lab and is the same as the companion analysis. Neurons were selected as in Zang et al.:

  • regions: 16 regions of interest (ROIs) built from Beryl areas;
  • task-window firing rate > 1 Hz;
  • presence ratio > 0.95.

Trials needed complete events and a response time of 0.08–2 s. All trials were kept. The paper’s first-400 cut was a sensitivity check and changed nothing (Figure 3, top right).

3.2 Metrics

Firing rate (FR) is the mean spike count in a 100 ms window divided by 0.1 s.

FF is the mean-subtracted Fano factor of Zang et al., following Churchland et al. 2011:

  • each trial’s spike count in a 100 ms window minus the mean count for its signed-contrast condition (9 conditions);
  • the variance of these pooled residuals, divided by the mean count.

Windows: pre-stimulus [−0.10, 0] s and post-stimulus [0.16, 0.26] s around stimulus onset. Quench = post FF − pre FF; negative values mean quenching.

Change from the paper: the residual variance divides by (n − number of conditions). Each condition mean uses up one degree of freedom, and this matters for the small trial subsets used below. At about 400 trials it is negligible.

3.3 Diagnostics that shaped the plan

FF depends on trial count. Median FF rises with the number of trials used (Figure 3, top), because more trials span more session time and slow drift adds variance. So every comparison between trial sets uses the same number of trials, drawn at random 20 times and averaged.

Engaged vs disengaged comparisons are confounded by time in session. This part is “Part A” below. Only 20 bwm and 7 lifespan exploration sessions had at least 20 disengaged trials. Engaged trials from early and late in a session differ from each other about as much as engaged and disengaged trials do, even though the state is the same (placebo, Figure 3 bottom). Part A was therefore kept descriptive. It showed no consistent state effect: on disengaged trials quenching was slightly weaker in bwm (+0.035) but slightly stronger in lifespan sessions (−0.045).

The paper’s post window mostly follows movement. Median first movement comes 0.14 s (bwm) or 0.12 s (lifespan) after stimulus onset, and 84% of trials move before the post window ends. On engaged bwm trials, most of the FF drop in that window is tied to movement (Figure 4): early movers show it, late movers barely do.

We therefore added a movement-safe variant: post window [0.02, 0.12] s, using only trials whose first movement came after 0.12 s. It keeps about 70% of trials and quenches as strongly as other early windows. It was chosen on bwm mice only, without looking at age.

3.4 Age effects on engaged trials, exploration set

Each neuron’s metrics were computed on two trial sets of the same size:

  • engaged: P(engaged) > 0.8;
  • all: trials of any state, which is what the paper’s analysis sees.

The sets have 150 trials (paper windows) or 100 trials (movement-safe window). The age effect, β_age, is the OLS slope of the metric on mouse mean age (per 100 days), with ROI fixed effects. FR and FF are on a log scale, as in the paper.

The mouse is the independent unit: p-values come from permuting age across mice, with each mouse’s neurons kept together. Zang et al. treated neurons as the unit, which gives much narrower intervals.

In exploration, β_age on engaged trials was almost the same as on all trials for every metric (Figure 5). The age effects themselves were weak at the mouse level (z ≤ 1.7).

3.5 Revised question

Restricted to engaged trials, with equal trial counts, are the age effects of Zang et al. on quenching, firing rate and Fano factor still present? And how much of each age effect disappears when disengaged trials are removed?

4 Locked analysis plan

All tests use confirmation mice and engaged trials (P(engaged) > 0.8, equal N per neuron). The statistic is β_age with ROI fixed effects, and p-values come from 10,000 permutations of age across mice.

Primary family Q (Holm correction across 3 tests; one-sided, less quenching with age):

test window trials per neuron scope
C1 paper 150 within-lab (one lab, both cohorts)
C2 paper 150 all labs
C3 movement-safe 100 all labs

Secondary family F (Holm correction across 4 tests; paper windows, all labs; added by the user):

test metric alternative
F1 pre-stimulus FR one-sided, higher with age
F2 post-stimulus FR one-sided, higher with age
F3 post-stimulus FF one-sided, higher with age
F4 pre-stimulus FF two-sided (the paper found no effect)

Mediation (descriptive). Δ = β_all − β_eng is the part of the age slope that disappears when disengaged trials are removed. It is estimated with a 95% mouse-bootstrap CI, using the same neurons in both trial sets.

Interpretation rules, fixed in advance:

  • “Also when engaged” holds if any Q test is significant.
  • “Not explained by disengagement” holds if, in addition, the upper bound of C2’s Δ is below 0.5 × β_all.

An earlier rule based on the ratio β_eng/β_all was replaced before unblinding. On exploration mice the ratio’s CI was uninformative (−1.1 to 2.5) because β_all’s CI included 0.

5 Results of confirmatory analysis

All three quenching tests were significant: quenching is weaker in older mice on engaged trials.

test β_age per 100 d z Holm p
C1, within-lab (18 mice) 0.029 2.4 0.011
C2, all labs (100 mice) 0.031 3.0 0.011
C3, movement-safe window 0.021 2.4 0.011

Removing disengaged trials did not reduce the effect. For C2, Δ = −0.003 (95% CI −0.009 to 0.002) against β_all = 0.029, so the pre-set criterion is met.

In the secondary family, post-stimulus FF rose with age (F3: z = 2.8, Holm p = 0.020), as Zang et al. report. Pre- and post-stimulus firing rate were in the paper’s direction but not significant (z ≈ 1.2, Holm p = 0.34). Pre-stimulus FF showed no effect (p = 0.42), which is consistent with the paper but doesn’t prove absence.

For every metric, window and scope, Δ was within ±0.005 of zero. Restricting to engaged trials left every age slope essentially unchanged.

6 Post-hoc analyses

These were requested by the user after unblinding and are not part of the locked plan. They have no multiplicity correction.

Within cohort (confirmation mice, engaged trials). Within bwm alone (89 mice, 116–429 d), quenching weakened with age:

  • paper window: β = 0.039 per 100 d, two-sided p = 0.066;
  • movement-safe window: β = 0.057, p = 0.003.

Post-stimulus FF rose (β = 0.042, p = 0.033). Within lifespan alone (11–12 mice) the slopes pointed the same way but were not significant. So the effect is not only a difference between cohorts; it is graded within the younger cohort too.

Per ROI (all 158 mice, paper windows, engaged trials; ROIs with at least 3 mice per cohort). β_age for quenching was positive in 15 of 16 ROIs, and its CI excluded 0 in LP, LS and SCm. Zang et al. named LP and LS among their strongest regions. Post-FF effects were more mixed across regions.

7 Discussion

Answer. Older mice show weaker quenching also when they are engaged. The age effect on quenching is the same on engaged trials as on all trials, and on the few sessions where engaged and disengaged trials could be compared directly, disengaged trials did not quench less in older mice. More time spent disengaged therefore cannot explain the effect. The higher post-stimulus FF also holds on engaged trials. The higher firing rate does not reach significance at the mouse level.

Relation to prior work.

  • The quenching and post-FF effects replicate Zang et al. under stricter conditions: mice rather than neurons as the unit, engaged trials only, equal trial counts.
  • They survive a window that excludes movement.
  • The FR effect did not: Zang et al. reported it at the neuron level, and with mice as the unit its slope is positive but within the permutation spread.

Caveats.

  • Age and cohort are confounded. The post hoc within-bwm slope supports a graded age effect, but lab, rig and region mix still differ between cohorts.
  • “Engaged” differs by age. In older mice the engaged state has a weaker stimulus weight, so “engaged” is a model-defined state, not an equal level of attention.
  • Part A is weak. Only 7 lifespan sessions could be used, and the early-vs-late placebo showed drift as large as the state differences.
  • Movement. Most of the FF drop in the paper’s window is tied to movement. The movement-safe result is smaller (β 0.021 vs 0.031), so part of the paper-window effect may reflect movement timing, which differs with age.
  • Not independent. Zang et al. analysed these same sessions, so the all-trial age effects are not independent evidence. Only the engaged-trial comparison is new.
  • Region coverage. Lifespan mice lack several regions, and ROI fixed effects adjust only the level of each region, not its age slope.

Lessons for AI-assisted analysis.

  • Check how FF depends on trial count, and use a time-in-session placebo, before comparing trial subsets.
  • Check movement timing against analysis windows taken from a paper.
  • Prefer a difference (Δ) over a ratio when the denominator can be near zero; that decision was made before unblinding.
